lessons.title: Write and Represent Inequalities
lessons.objective: I can write inequalities to represent real-world situations.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my inequality using the words inequality, greater than, less than, and at least / at most.

concept.heading: How do I write an inequality from words?
concept.intro: An inequality compares two amounts using <, >, ≤, or ≥. I use one when many values are allowed, not just one. I pick a variable and match the words to the right symbol.
concept.keyIdea: Writing & Representing Inequalities. Formula: < (less) | > (greater) | ≤ (at most / ≤) | ≥ (at least / ≥). 1. 'At least', 'minimum', 'no less than' translate to ≥ (greater than or equal to). 2. 'At most', 'maximum', 'no more than' translate to ≤ (less than or equal to). 3. 'More than' is >; 'Fewer than' / 'Less than' is <

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Clue: 'The suspect is at least 18 years old.'
I let a stand for the age. 'At least 18' means 18 or more.
'At least' includes 18, so I use the symbol ≥.
My inequality is a ≥ 18. So a could be 18, 19, 20, and up.
linesEs: Pista: «El sospechoso tiene al menos 18 años.»
Dejo que a represente la edad. «Al menos 18» significa 18 o más.
«Al menos» incluye el 18, así que uso el símbolo ≥.
Mi desigualdad es a ≥ 18. Entonces a podría ser 18, 19, 20 y más.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Clue: 'A bag holds fewer than 10 items.' What does 'fewer than' mean?
It means less than, and it does NOT include 10, so we use <.
We let n be the number of items: n < 10.
linesEs: Pista: «Una bolsa lleva menos de 10 artículos.» ¿Qué significa «menos de»?
Significa menor que, y no incluye el 10, así que usamos <.
Dejamos que n sea el número de artículos: n < 10.

vocabulary.definition: Represent a range of possible values with <, >, ≤, or ≥.
vocabulary.example: You must be at least 12 years old: a ≥ 12.

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence that compares two sides with <, >, ≤, or ≥.
vocabulary.example: x > 5 means x can be 6, 7, 8, ... — any number greater than 5

vocabulary.definition: The > sign, showing one number is bigger.
vocabulary.example: 8 > 3 — eight is larger than three

vocabulary.definition: The < sign, showing one number is smaller.
vocabulary.example: 2 < 7 — two is smaller than seven

vocabulary.definition: 'At least' means ≥. 'At most' means ≤.
vocabulary.example: 'At least 10 players' → p ≥ 10 (could be 10, 11, 12, ...); 'At most 5 tries' → t ≤ 5 (could be 5, 4, 3, ...)

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for a number that is unknown or can change.
vocabulary.example: In x > 5, the letter x stands for any number greater than 5.

vocabulary.definition: A phrase meaning less than or equal to (≤).
vocabulary.example: “No more than 8 people” means people ≤ 8.

vocabulary.definition: A limit that a solution must satisfy.
vocabulary.example: A voter must be 18 or older.

vocabulary.definition: All the values that make an inequality true.
vocabulary.example: Every number 7 or below.

lessons.title: Understand Inequalities and Their Solutions
lessons.objective: I can graph the solutions of an inequality on a number line.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my graph using the words number line, open circle, closed circle, and solution set.

concept.heading: How do I graph an inequality on a number line?
concept.intro: Graphing an inequality shows every value that makes it true. I draw a circle at the boundary number and shade the side that works. The circle tells me if the boundary is included.
concept.keyIdea: Graphing Inequalities on the Number Line. 1. Draw the boundary circle at the given constant number. 2. Open Circle (○) for < or > (boundary value is not included in solution set). 3. Closed Circle (●) for ≤ or ≥ (boundary value is included). Shade right for >, left for <

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Graph t ≥ 2. The boundary number is 2.
The symbol ≥ includes 2, so I draw a closed (filled) circle at 2.
'Greater than or equal to' means larger values work, so I shade to the right.
Now the graph shows 2, 3, 4, and every value above 2.
linesEs: Grafica t ≥ 2. El número límite es 2.
El símbolo ≥ incluye el 2, así que dibujo un círculo cerrado (relleno) en 2.
«Mayor o igual que» significa que sirven los valores más grandes, así que sombreo a la derecha.
Ahora la gráfica muestra el 2, el 3, el 4 y todos los valores arriba de 2.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Graph x < 5. What number is the boundary?
The symbol < does NOT include 5, so we use an open (empty) circle at 5.
Which way do we shade for 'less than'? To the left, toward smaller numbers.
linesEs: Grafica x < 5. ¿Cuál número es el límite?
El símbolo < no incluye el 5, así que usamos un círculo abierto (vacío) en 5.
¿Hacia dónde sombreamos para «menor que»? A la izquierda, hacia los números más pequeños.

vocabulary.definition: Show every solution to an inequality on a number line with a boundary point and an arrow.
vocabulary.example: x > 3 uses an open circle at 3 and an arrow to the right.

vocabulary.definition: A straight line where numbers are placed in order; numbers get smaller to the left and larger to the right.
vocabulary.example: A horizontal line with marks at 0, 1, 2, 3, ... showing where values fall

vocabulary.definition: An empty circle showing a number is NOT included.
vocabulary.example: x > 5: open circle at 5 means 5 itself is NOT a solution, but 5.1, 6, 7, ... are

vocabulary.definition: A filled-in circle showing a number IS included.
vocabulary.example: x ≥ 5: closed circle at 5 means 5 IS a solution, and so are 6, 7, 8, ...

vocabulary.definition: All the numbers that make the inequality true.
vocabulary.example: For x > 3, the solution set includes 3.1, 4, 5, 10, 100 — any number greater than 3

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence that compares two sides with <, >, ≤, or ≥.
vocabulary.example: x ≥ 3 is an inequality; it is graphed as a closed circle on 3 with an arrow to the right.

vocabulary.definition: The number on the number line where the solution set starts.
vocabulary.example: For x > 5, the boundary point is 5, shown with an open circle.

vocabulary.definition: A sentence that the numbers make correct.
vocabulary.example: 9 > 5 is true.

title: Entry Rules Arcade
mission: Write fair entry rules for an arcade. Use inequality symbols and decide whether a boundary value is allowed.
investigate: Compare x > 12 with x ≥ 12. Test the boundary value itself.
Show several different values that satisfy one rule.
Explain why an inequality usually has many solutions rather than one.
create: Write two entry rules: one includes its boundary and one excludes it. Give words, symbols, number-line graphs, and examples and nonexamples for each.

support.prompt: Which inequality represents: 'The temperature is less than 40 degrees'?
support.explanation: 'Less than' means <, so the inequality is t < 40.
feedback: Your symbol opens toward temperatures ABOVE 40. 'Less than 40' lives on the other side — which way should the symbol point?
The ≤ symbol lets the temperature be exactly 40. 'Less than 40' leaves 40 out.
An equals sign pins the temperature to a single value, but this situation describes a whole range of temperatures.
hints: Find the comparison phrase: 'less than 40 degrees'. Does 40 itself count, or only temperatures below it?
'Less than' with no 'or equal to' means a strict symbol — no bar underneath — pointing toward the smaller side.
Test a value: is 35 degrees 'less than 40'? Yes — so pick the strict symbol that puts t on the smaller side of 40.

support.prompt: Which inequality represents: 'You must be at least 48 inches tall to ride'?
support.explanation: 'At least' means greater than or equal to, so h ≥ 48.
feedback: So close — test the boundary. Does a rider who is EXACTLY 48 inches tall get to ride? Your strict symbol turns that rider away.
This describes riders who are too short to ride. Check which direction the symbol opens.
This would let anyone shorter than 48 inches ride. 'At least 48' makes 48 the smallest allowed height, not the largest.
hints: 'At least 48' — ask yourself: can a rider who is EXACTLY 48 inches tall ride? That decides whether 48 is included.
When the boundary value is allowed, you need a symbol with the 'or equal to' bar under it.
Allowed heights are 48, 49, 50, and up. Pick the symbol that includes 48 itself AND points toward bigger numbers.

support.prompt: Which inequality represents: 'A store can hold no more than 75 people'?
support.explanation: 'No more than' means less than or equal to, so p ≤ 75.
feedback: Almost — check the boundary. Is a store holding EXACTLY 75 people breaking the rule? Your symbol says yes; re-read 'no more than.'
This says the store always holds 75 or more people, which is the opposite of a limit. 'No more than' caps the number.
This describes crowds larger than the limit. 'No more than 75' means the store never goes above 75.
hints: 'No more than 75' — could the store hold exactly 75 people? Could it hold 76?
'No more than' allows the boundary but nothing above it — that calls for a symbol with the 'or equal' bar.
Test values: 75 people is fine, 76 is not. Pick the symbol that keeps p at 75 or below.

support.prompt: Which inequality represents: 'The speed limit is more than 25 mph'?
support.explanation: 'More than' means strictly greater than, so s > 25.
feedback: Test the boundary value: is 25 itself 'more than 25'? Your symbol includes it — decide whether the words allow that.
The symbol points the wrong way. 'More than' describes speeds above 25, not below it.
An equals sign names one exact speed, but 'more than 25' covers every speed above 25.
hints: 'More than 25' — is exactly 25 included, or only speeds above 25?
'More than' (not 'at least') is strict — no 'or equal' bar under the symbol.
Test: 26 works, but 25 itself does not. Pick the strict symbol that puts s above 25.

steps: Clue: The witness says the suspect is at least 16 years old.
Choose a variable: Let a stand for the suspect's age.
Write the inequality: a > 16
support.explanation: 'At least 16' means 16 itself counts as meeting the clue, plus any age older than 16. The symbol > would leave out exactly 16, so the correct inequality is a ≥ 16, not a > 16.
hints: Does 'at least 16' allow the suspect's age to be exactly 16, or must it be older?
'At least' means the boundary age itself satisfies the clue. Pick the symbol family that keeps 16 as a solution.

support.explanation: x < 5 means 5 is NOT included (open circle) and values less than 5 are shaded (left).
feedback: The direction is right, but < does not include 5, so the circle stays open.
This shades the values above 5. Test a number like 7 in x < 5 and see whether it belongs in the solution set.
This both fills in 5 and shades the larger side. Try x = 5 and x = 7 in the inequality — check whether either one makes it true.
hints: Every inequality graph asks two questions: is 5 itself a solution (circle type), and which side holds the solutions (shading)?
Strict symbols like < exclude the boundary, so check whether 5 makes x < 5 true. Then shade toward test values that work.
First step: 5 < 5 is false, so 5 is NOT included — that fixes the circle type. Now test x = 4 to find the shading direction.

support.explanation: x ≥ 3 means 3 IS included (closed circle) and values greater than or equal to 3 are shaded (right).
feedback: The direction is right, but ≥ includes 3, so the circle should be filled in.
This shades the numbers below 3. Test x = 1 in x ≥ 3 to see whether small values satisfy the inequality.
This leaves 3 out and shades the smaller side. Check whether x = 3 makes x ≥ 3 true, and test x = 1 as well.
hints: Check the symbol: ≥ has the 'or equal' bar. What does that bar mean for the circle at 3?
The bar means 3 IS a solution, so the circle gets filled in. Then a quick test value tells you the shading side.
First step: 3 ≥ 3 is true, so 3 is included. Now test x = 10 — is 10 ≥ 3 true? Shade toward that side.

support.explanation: x > 8 means 8 is NOT included (open circle) and values greater than 8 are shaded to the right.
feedback: The direction is right, but > does not include 8, so the circle stays open.
This shades the values below 8. Substitute x = 4 into x > 8 and check whether it works.
This fills in 8 and shades the smaller side. Try x = 8 and x = 4 in x > 8 and see whether either one belongs.
hints: Two decisions: does x = 8 make x > 8 true, and are the solutions bigger or smaller than 8?
Symbols without the 'or equal' bar exclude the boundary. Then shade only the side where test numbers make the statement true.
First step: 8 > 8 is false, so 8 is NOT included — that fixes your circle. Now test x = 9 to pick the shading side.

support.explanation: x ≤ 10 means 10 IS included (closed circle) and values less than or equal to 10 are shaded (left).
feedback: The direction is right, but ≤ includes 10, so the circle should be filled in.
This shades the numbers above 10. Test x = 12 in x ≤ 10 and see whether large values are allowed.
This excludes 10 and shades the larger side. Check whether x = 10 satisfies x ≤ 10, then test x = 12 too.
hints: Ask two things: does 10 itself satisfy x ≤ 10, and do solutions live above or below 10?
The 'or equal' bar means the boundary is a solution — that decides the circle. A test value decides the shading.
First step: 10 ≤ 10 is true, so 10 is included. Now test x = 3 — is 3 ≤ 10 true? Shade toward the side that works.

steps: Read: Graph n ≥ 8 on the number line.
Circle choice: Open circle at 8
Shade direction: Shade right
Final graph: Open circle at 8, shaded right
support.explanation: n ≥ 8 uses ≥, which means 8 IS part of the solution set. The circle must be CLOSED (filled in), not open — the shading to the right is correct. Final graph: closed circle at 8, shaded right.
hints: Look at the symbol: does it have a small line under it, like ≤ or ≥?
≥ and ≤ always use a closed, filled-in circle because the boundary number counts as a solution.

support.prompt: Predict the test value for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: x ≥ 12; x = 10 does not qualify. Closed circle at 12: the boundary is included.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.

core.prompt: A parking garage charges if your stay is more than 2 hours. Which inequality represents times t that are charged?
core.explanation: 'More than 2 hours' means strictly greater than: t > 2. Exactly 2 hours is not charged.
feedback: Think about the driver who stays exactly 2 hours. Your symbol charges them — does 'more than 2 hours' include exactly 2?
This describes short stays, which are not charged. Check which side of 2 the symbol opens toward.
This would charge a stay of exactly 2 hours, and it also covers shorter stays. 'More than 2' leaves 2 out and looks above it.
hints: The charge starts once the stay goes PAST 2 hours. Is a stay of exactly 2 hours charged?
If exactly 2 hours is NOT charged, the boundary is excluded — that rules out any symbol with the 'or equal' bar.
Test t = 2 and t = 3: only stays longer than 2 are charged. Pick the symbol that makes t = 3 true but t = 2 false.

steps: Clue: The report says no fewer than 9 witnesses saw the suspect.
Choose a variable: Let w stand for the number of witnesses.
Write the inequality: w < 9
core.explanation: 'No fewer than 9' means the count cannot drop below 9 — 9 or more witnesses is required. That is w ≥ 9, not w < 9, which would only allow numbers below 9, the opposite of what the clue says.
hints: Does 'no fewer than 9' rule out having 9 witnesses, or does it rule out having fewer than 9?
'No fewer than 9' says 9 itself is acceptable — only counts BELOW 9 break the rule. Choose the symbol that keeps 9 in.

core.prompt: A number line shows a closed circle at 8 and is shaded to the left. Which inequality does this represent?
core.explanation: Closed circle means the value is included (≤ or ≥). Shaded left means less than or equal to: x ≤ 8.
feedback: Your direction matches the shading — the circle is the clue you skipped. A filled-in circle answers one question: is 8 itself a solution?
This symbol points the solutions toward the larger numbers, but the graph is shaded toward the smaller ones. Match the shading direction to the symbol before choosing.
This symbol leaves 8 out and points toward larger values, while the graph shows a filled circle and shading to the left. Line up both features.
hints: Read the graph's two clues: the circle at 8 is CLOSED, and the shading runs LEFT toward smaller numbers.
A closed circle means 8 itself is a solution, so the symbol needs the 'or equal' bar. Shading left means solutions are 8 or smaller.
Test x = 5 (in the shaded part) and x = 8 (the circle): both must make the inequality true. Which choice passes both tests?

steps: Read: The case file needs fewer than 9 clues, so c < 9. Graph it.
Circle choice: Open circle at 9
Shade direction: Shade right
Final graph: Open circle at 9, shaded right
core.explanation: The circle choice was correct — c < 9 does not include 9, so it needs an open circle. But 'less than' means smaller values, so the shading should go LEFT toward smaller numbers, not right. Final graph: open circle at 9, shaded left.
hints: The circle type and the shading direction are two separate decisions — check both.
< and ≤ shade LEFT toward smaller values. > and ≥ shade RIGHT toward larger values.

steps: Situation: No more than 25 students can join the field trip
Identify key phrase: 'No more than' means greater than
Write inequality: s > 25
stretch.explanation: 'No more than' means less than or equal to (≤), not greater than. The correct inequality is s ≤ 25.
hints: 'No more than 25' means the number cannot exceed 25. Is that greater than or less than or equal to?
'No more than 25' sets a ceiling that 25 itself satisfies. Test the boundary: should s = 25 be a solution of your inequality?

stretch.prompt: Write two different real-world situations: one that uses > and one that uses ≥. Explain why the situations need different symbols even though both mean 'bigger.'
stretch.frame: Situation 1 (>): ___. This uses > because ___. Situation 2 (≥): ___. This uses ≥ because ___. The difference is that ≥ includes ___ while > does not.
stretch.explanation: The only difference between > and ≥ is whether the boundary number itself is allowed. A rule like "score more than 10 points to win" leaves 10 out, so it needs >, while "you must be at least 13 to watch" lets exactly 13 count, so it needs ≥. Testing the boundary number in your own situation is the quickest way to check which symbol fits.
hints: The whole difference between > and ≥ is the boundary number itself: one includes it, one leaves it out.
Pick real rules: 'score more than 10 points to win' (strict) versus 'you must be at least 13 to watch' (boundary counts). Explain each choice.
Write situation 1 with 'more than' and test its boundary number — it should fail. Write situation 2 with 'at least' and test — the boundary should pass.

steps: Inequality: x > 6
Circle type: Closed circle at 6
Shade direction: Shade right
Graph: Closed circle at 6, shaded right
stretch.explanation: x > 6 uses a strict inequality (no 'equal to'), so the circle should be OPEN, not closed. Open circle at 6, shaded right.
hints: Look at the inequality symbol carefully. Is it > or ≥?
> means strictly greater than — 6 is NOT included, so the circle must be open.

stretch.prompt: A theme park has two rides. Ride A requires height h > 48 inches. Ride B requires height h ≥ 48 inches. A child is exactly 48 inches tall. Which ride can they go on? Explain using number line graphs for both inequalities.
stretch.frame: For Ride A (h > 48), the graph has a ___ circle at 48. Since 48 > 48 is ___, the child ___ ride A. For Ride B (h ≥ 48), the graph has a ___ circle at 48. Since 48 ≥ 48 is ___, the child ___ ride B.
stretch.explanation: The child is exactly on the boundary, so test 48 in each rule. For Ride A, 48 > 48 is false, so the graph has an open circle at 48 and the child cannot ride. For Ride B, 48 ≥ 48 is true, so the graph has a closed circle at 48 and the child can ride B.
hints: The child is EXACTLY 48 inches — right on the boundary. The two rides treat that boundary number differently.
Test h = 48 in each rule: is 48 > 48 true or false? Is 48 ≥ 48 true or false? Each graph's circle type shows the same story.
Start with Ride A: 48 > 48 is false, so its graph has an open circle at 48 and 48 is left out. Now test Ride B's rule the same way.
